patches_submitted.subject: [PATCH] btrfs: downgrade the reflink source inode lock

version_history.subject: [PATCH] btrfs: downgrade the reflink source inode lock

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch modifies the Btrfs file system to downgrade the lock on the source inode during a reflink operation from exclusive to shared, reducing contention and improving performance. The change also adds a flag to indicate when an inode is being used as a reflink source, which allows direct I/O writes to take the VFS inode lock in shared mode instead of exclusive mode. This patch was tested with concurrent readers and writers and showed significant latency improvements.

review_comments.author: Filipe Manana
review_comments.summary:
Reviewer noted that taking the inode's rwsem in shared mode during reflink may not provide significant benefits if only a portion of the file is being reflinked and direct IO reads occur on a different range, requesting clarification in the change log.

Filipe Manana noted that direct IO reads and writes increment the i_dio_count by calling inode_dio_begin(), which may lead to issues, and suggested this as a valid concern
review_comments.raw_body:
You mean a direct IO read operation happening in parallel with a
reflink using the same file as a source right?
And reflinking the entire file?

Because we only take the VFS lock (rwsem in struct inode) for direct IO reads.

However during reads (both direct IO and buffered) we always lock the
extent range in the inode's extent io tree, and the reflink also locks
the range.
So taking the rwsem in shared mode won't help much unless we are not
reflinking the whole file and direct IO reads happen on a different
range.
I think that should be explicit in the change log.

---

https://sashiko.dev/#/patchset/65fa79581e1d29d6d6fabae71d23e741bff0ddf9.1788974902.git.boris%40bur.io

As every direct IO read and write increment i_dio_count with a call to
inode_dio_begin() in iomap.

Thanks.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/5] mm/mempolicy: add mempolicy_create()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function, mempolicy_create(), which creates and validates a memory policy without installing it into the current task's policy. The function takes mode, flags, and nodes as arguments, allocates a new policy, constrains it to the task's cpuset, and returns the policy or an error pointer on failure. This patch also exports the symbol for use in guest_memfd integration with KVM.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 2/5] mm/mempolicy: add mpol_set_shared_policy_range()
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new function mpol_set_shared_policy_range() that allows installing an already-built memory policy over an arbitrary page range without requiring a VMA. The existing mpol_set_shared_policy() function is reimplemented as a thin wrapper to derive the range from the VMA, allowing both functions to share a single underlying path. This change addresses limitations in the current implementation that make it unusable for binding entire backing inodes from in-kernel code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/5] KVM: guest_memfd: bind backing memory to a NUMA node at creation
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new flag called GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE to the KVM guest memory file descriptor (memfd) feature. When this flag is set, the backing memory for the guest is bound to a specific NUMA node at creation time, rather than being allocated through a shared mempolicy that can be modified later. This change requires CONFIG_NUMA to be enabled and only allows binding to nodes within the calling task's cpuset. The policy is fixed for the life of the fd and cannot be rebound on later cpuset changes.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 4/5] selftests: KVM: guest_memfd: let the gmem_test() harness bind a node
series_items.patch_summary: This patch extends the create_guest_memfd() function to accept a node argument, allowing the gmem_test() harness to bind a node when creating a guest memory file descriptor. The BIND_NODE flag is used to determine whether the node argument should be ignored or used for binding. This change enables testing of GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE functionality.

series_items.subject: [PATCH 5/5] selftests: KVM: guest_memfd: test GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds tests for the GUEST_MEMFD_FLAG_BIND_NODE flag in KVM's guest_memfd feature. The tests cover various scenarios, including single and multi-node systems, invalid arguments, and edge cases such as non-zero padding and out-of-range node numbers. The tests ensure that the BIND_NODE flag behaves correctly when used with other flags and when faults occur on remote nodes.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series adds a new flag to the KVM guest memory file descriptor (memfd) API, allowing users to bind the backing memory of the guest to a specific NUMA node. This is done by creating an MPOL_BIND policy for the requested node and installing it over the whole inode, ensuring that every folio is allocated on the specified node without requiring user-space mbind(). The patch series also includes self-test harness support and testing to validate the new functionality. The approach taken is to simplify the guest NUMA topology by binding a single fd to a host node, rather than interleaving it across multiple nodes, which would defeat placement decisions made by the guest.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 1/7] nfsdctl: sync nfsd_netlink.h with the kernel
series_items.patch_summary: This patch updates the nfsd_netlink.h file in the nfs-utils package to match the latest version from the kernel. It imports new attributes related to rpcbind registration, including NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_USERSPACE_RPCBIND and NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_RPCBIND. The patch also adds a test for these new attributes and bumps the USE_SYSTEM_NFSD_NETLINK_H probe to one of the new attributes. This change is necessary because some hosts may have headers that are newer than v6.9, which introduced NFSD_CMD_SERVER_STATS_GET.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 2/7] nfsdctl: probe the policy of any command
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl utility to probe the policy of any command, not just THREADS_SET. It introduces a new function query_nfsd_nl_cmd_policy() that takes the command number as an argument and writes the highest attribute through its callback argument. The original query_nfsd_nl_policy() function is preserved for backwards compatibility and still probes THREADS_SET. No functional changes are made, but the code is refactored to make it more flexible and reusable.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 3/7] nfsdctl: share the listener nest parser
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the listener nest parser in nfsdctl to improve code organization and efficiency. The existing parse_listener_get function is split into two functions: parse_sock_nest, which unpacks a NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_ADDR nest, and the original parse_listener_get function, which now only iterates over top-level attributes. This change allows for better handling of mixed attribute replies and prevents counting non-listener attributes as listeners. The patch makes no functional changes to the code's behavior.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 4/7] nfsdctl: add rpcbind registration helpers
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds rpcbind registration helpers to the nfsdctl utility, allowing it to register and unregister NFS services with the local rpcbind. The code ensures that only valid registrations are made, based on rules defined by the kernel's behavior. The patch also moves the struct server_socket definition to a new header file and updates the Makefile to include the new files.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 5/7] nfsdctl: register nfsd listeners with rpcbind
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl utility to register NFS and NFSACL listeners with the local rpcbind instead of the kernel. This change addresses a problem where a slow rpcbind could block other NFSD netlink commands due to synchronous calls made by the kernel while holding an internal mutex. The new approach involves sending a flag, reading the reply, and then registering the listeners without holding any locks. The patch also includes support for detecting whether the kernel supports this feature and handles cases where registration fails or is not supported.

series_items.subject: [PATCH RFC nfs-utils 6/7] nfsdctl: clear rpcbind entries when the last thread stops
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the nfsdctl command to clear rpcbind entries when the last thread stops. The previous behavior was incorrect, as it relied on a kernel function that is no longer used. The patch fixes this issue by checking if all threads have stopped and clearing the rpcbind entries only then. This ensures that the rpcbind entries do not outlive the server and point to an unused port.

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary: Identified an issue with the wording of the documentation, suggesting that it should accurately describe what listeners are omitted from the reply. Also pointed out a potential regression in the handling of RDMA transport.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, 10 Sep 2026, Jeff Layton wrote:
> Describe the interface that lets a caller take over rpcbind registration.

> --- a/Documentation/netlink/specs/nfsd.yaml
> +++ b/Documentation/netlink/specs/nfsd.yaml
> @@ -483,13 +527,22 @@ operations:
>      -
>        name: listener-set
> -      doc: set nfs running sockets
> +      doc: >-
> +        set nfs running sockets. A request that carries userspace-rpcbind
> +        is answered with a reply rather than a bare ack, and the addr list
> +        in that reply names only the listeners that have an rpcbind netid.

"listeners that have an rpcbind netid" overstates the set. RDMA
listeners have netids (rdma, rdma6) but are omitted from the
reply.

Following the way Solaris handles RDMA transport, NFSD never
registered RDMA itself, so that is not a regression, but the doc
should say what your filter actually selects.


>        attribute-set: server-sock
>        flags: [admin-perm]
>        do:
>          request:
>            attributes:
>              - addr
> +            - userspace-rpcbind
> +        reply:
> +          attributes:
> +            - addr
> +            - userspace-rpcbind
> +            - rpcbind

The spec declares an unconditional reply, but patch 4 sends one only
when the request carried userspace-rpcbind. ynl has no way to express
a conditional reply, and no other in-tree spec does this.

Either always send the reply (drop the userspace_rpcbind gate in
patch 4, so a plain caller simply ignores it), or leave listener-set
without a reply and put the registration data in a separate get
operation. I lean toward always replying; that's is a little more
"declarative".


-- 
Chuck Lever (Come to NFS bake-a-thon! https://nfsv4bat.org)

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary: Identified a potential issue where the ownership check in the netlink path is not enforced consistently. Suggested moving the mismatch test into nfsd_create_serv() to ensure both paths agree.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Thu, 10 Sep 2026, Jeff Layton wrote:

> --- a/fs/nfsd/nfsctl.c
> +++ b/fs/nfsd/nfsctl.c
> @@ -2111,15 +2112,25 @@ int nfsd_nl_listener_set_doit(struct sk_buff *skb, struct genl_info *info)
> +	userspace_rpcbind = nla_get_flag(info->attrs[NFSD_A_SERVER_SOCK_USERSPACE_RPCBIND]);
> +
>  	mutex_lock(&nfsd_mutex);
>  
> -	err = nfsd_create_serv(net);
> +	nn = net_generic(net, nfsd_net_id);
> +
> +	if (nn->nfsd_serv && nn->nfsd_serv->sv_no_rpcbind != userspace_rpcbind) {
> +		NL_SET_ERR_MSG(info->extack,
> +			       "cannot change rpcbind ownership while a server exists");
> +		mutex_unlock(&nfsd_mutex);
> +		return -EBUSY;
> +	}
> +
> +	err = nfsd_create_serv(net, userspace_rpcbind);

This ownership check lives only in the netlink path, so it is
enforced in one direction. Consider: the serv is created here with
userspace-rpcbind, then an old rpc.nfsd writes a socket fd to
/proc/fs/nfsd/portlist. __write_ports_addfd() calls
nfsd_create_serv(net, false), which returns 0 at the existing
"if (nn->nfsd_serv) return 0;" without looking at the flag.
svc_addsock() then goes through svc_setup_socket() with pmap_register
set, and svc_register() returns 0 early because sv_no_rpcbind is set.
The write succeeds, and the new listener is neither registered by the
kernel nor reported to the userspace owner. The reverse order gets
-EBUSY from the check above.

Moving the mismatch test into nfsd_create_serv(), where every creator
already funnels, would make both paths agree. The extack message would
need a different home, but the errno is the important part.


-- 
Chuck Lever (Come to NFS bake-a-thon! https://nfsv4bat.org)

review_comments.author: Chuck Lever
review_comments.summary:
The reviewer noted that after a partial failure in creating listeners, nfsd continues to serve on the first port created and does not send a reply to the caller, which was never informed about the programs to register or the listeners that came up. The reviewer suggested either tearing down the listeners when any of them fails or sending the reply whenever at least one listener exists.

Reviewer Chuck Lever pointed out that genlmsg_new() already includes GENL_HDRLEN in its size calculation, and suggested passing only the attribute payload to avoid double-counting.

The reviewer suggested extracting a helper function that emits one address nest for an xprt to avoid code duplication between nfsd_nl_listener_set_msg() and nfsd_nl_listener_get_doit(), and also noted that the XPT_RPCB_UNREG filter in nfsd_nl_listener_set_msg() only selects TCP and UDP, which should be reflected in the specification.

The reviewer noted that the ACL block in nfsd_support_acl_version() is redundant and can be removed, as it only handles a specific special case for the ACL program version.
review_comments.raw_body:
The second sentence of the comment is not true after a partial
failure. Take a request with userspace-rpcbind carrying {tcp:2049,
tcp:<port already in use>}. The creation loop continues past the
second failure and keeps only the last errno. The 2049 xprt is on
sv_permsocks, so the serv survives the list_empty() check below, but
this gate skips the reply and the caller sees -EADDRINUSE. nfsd is
now serving on 2049 with nothing registered in rpcbind, and the caller
was never told which listeners came up or which programs to register.
The same end state results when nfsd_nl_listener_set_msg() itself
fails with -ENOMEM.

In kernel-owned mode the survivor would already have been registered
inside svc_xprt_create_from_sa(), so this is a behavioral gap specific
to the new mode. Either tear down the listeners that were created when
any of them fails, or send the reply whenever at least one listener
exists on the serv, regardless of err. The second keeps the existing
partial-success semantics; the caller can then act on what it got.

---

genlmsg_new() already adds GENL_HDRLEN via genlmsg_total_size(), so
this term double-counts it. Harmless, but the comment will mislead the
next person sizing a reply. Pass only the attribute payload here.

---

This is the same nest emission as the loop in
nfsd_nl_listener_get_doit(), apart from the XPT_RPCB_UNREG filter and
the errno (that one returns -EINVAL). A small helper that emits one
addr nest for an xprt, called from both loops, would keep the two from
drifting, with the size accounting above as the third place to keep
in step.

Also, as noted on patch 2, this filter selects TCP and UDP only; the
spec doc should match.

---

The ACL block is redundant with the first test. The ACL program has
pg_nvers = NFSD_ACL_NRVERS and pg_vers = nfsd_acl_version, whose
slots 0 and 1 and any compiled-out version are NULL, and
nfsd_support_acl_version() checks exactly that range and that array.
Dropping the block removes the function's only program-number special
case and the #if with it.


-- 
Chuck Lever (Come to NFS bake-a-thon! https://nfsv4bat.org)

The patch removes the need for the kernel to look up who called it to make these decisions, instead allowing the caller to fill in the policy once per scan pass or call. This change simplifies the code and improves performance by reducing unnecessary checks.

The scan function reads the table under mmap_lock, while the run function performs the actual collapse. This change improves code organization and reduces complexity by separating these two tasks. Additionally, this patch introduces changes to tracing and khugepaged behavior, including new tracing events and adjustments to how file tables are handled.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series separates the collapse engine from its callers in the Linux kernel's memory management code. The current implementation has the collapse engine and its callers intertwined, making it difficult to understand and maintain. This patch series draws a clear boundary between the two by introducing an interface for the collapse engine and moving the syscall to madvise.c. The engine is now split into four calls: initialization, policy setup, scanning under mmap_lock, and running without mmap_lock. This change improves modularity, readability, and maintainability of the code.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v5 02/19] selftests/mm: skip collapse_compound_extreme() where the PMD is too large
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series introduces a selftest to verify the functionality of khugepaged, a kernel feature that allows for efficient handling of large memory pages. The test specifically targets the collapse_compound_extreme() function, which is responsible for building a PTE table full of distinct PTE-mapped compound pages. However, this function requires hpage_pmd_nr PMD-order allocations in a row, which can be unreliable when dealing with very large PMDs. To address this issue, the patch series introduces a skip condition to prevent collapse_compound_extreme() from running when the PMD is larger than 32M.

> compound pages by cycling hpage_pmd_nr fault-time THPs through mremap.  It

series_items.patch_summary: This patch series aims to improve the reliability of swapout operations in selftests/mm by addressing issues related to khugepaged and madvise(MADV_PAGEOUT). The changes include retrying madvise(MADV_PAGEOUT) multiple times, holding the range out of khugepaged's reach during the retry period, and skipping the swapout if it fails. The patch also introduces a new function `swapout_range` to handle the swapout operation.

> 
> collapse_swapin_single_pte() and collapse_max_ptes_swap() swap a range out
> and then require smaps to report exactly the count they asked for.  Two
> things keep that count from arriving.
> 
> MADV_PAGEOUT is best effort, so the count often turns up a moment late.
> 
> And wait_for_scan() leaves the range eligible for collapsing, so
> khugepaged is still working on it.  Collapsing reads the swapped-out pages
> back in, so the daemon empties the swap as fast as the case fills it.  On

From: "Kiryl Shutsemau (Meta)" <kas@kernel.org>

The khugepaged mTHP tests detect collapse results with the vm_util
folio-order helpers rather than smaps AnonHugePages, which only sees PMD
mappings.  If those helpers are wrong, every case built on them is wrong
the same way, and nothing says so.

memory in with only that order enabled.  Require the helpers to classify
the backing as exactly that order: not the order below it, and base-page
memory as order 0.

reported as itself rather than as a collapse failure.  Verified on x86-64

+// SPDX-License-Identifier: GPL-2.0
+/*
+ * Self-check for the vm_util folio-order helpers, is_backed_by_folio() and
+ * is_range_backed_by_order(), which the khugepaged mTHP cases use to detect
+ * collapse results.  For every anon THP order the kernel supports, fault
+ * memory in with only that order enabled and require the helpers to report
+ * exactly that order.
+ */
+#define _GNU_SOURCE
+#include <fcntl.h>
+#include <stdio.h>
+#include <stdlib.h>
+#include <sys/mman.h>
+#include <unistd.h>
+
+#include "kselftest.h"
+#include "vm_util.h"
+#include "hugepage_settings.h"
+
+static int pagemap_fd;
+static int kpageflags_fd;
+
+static char *alloc_aligned(size_t size)
+{
+	size_t len = size * 2;
+	char *p, *aligned;
+
+	p = mmap(NULL, len, PROT_READ | PROT_WRITE,
+		 MAP_ANONYMOUS | MAP_PRIVATE, -1, 0);
+	if (p == MAP_FAILED)
+		ksft_exit_fail_perror("mmap()");
+
+	aligned = (char *)ALIGN((uintptr_t)p, size);
+	if (aligned != p)
+		munmap(p, aligned - p);
+	if (aligned + size != p + len)
+		munmap(aligned + size, p + len - aligned - size);
+
+	return aligned;
+}
+
+static void check_order(int order)
+{
+	struct thp_settings settings = *thp_current_settings();
+	size_t size = psize() << order;
+	bool ok = true;
+	char *p;
+	int i;
+
+	for (i = 0; i < NR_ORDERS; i++)
+		settings.hugepages[i].enabled = THP_NEVER;
+	if (order)
+		settings.hugepages[order].enabled = THP_ALWAYS;
+	thp_push_settings(&settings);
+
+	p = alloc_aligned(size);
+	*p = 1;
+
+	if (!is_range_backed_by_order(p, size, order, pagemap_fd, kpageflags_fd)) {
+		ksft_print_msg("order %d not detected after fault\n", order);
+		ok = false;
+	}
+
+	/* A lower order must be rejected: the folio is larger */
+	if (order && is_range_backed_by_order(p, size, order - 1,
+					      pagemap_fd, kpageflags_fd)) {
+		ksft_print_msg("order %d also reported as order %d\n",
+			       order, order - 1);
+		ok = false;
+	}
+
+	/* A large folio must not pass as order 0 */
+	if (order && is_range_backed_by_order(p, size, 0,
+					      pagemap_fd, kpageflags_fd)) {
+		ksft_print_msg("order %d also reported as order 0\n", order);
+		ok = false;
+	}
+
+	munmap(p, size);
+	thp_pop_settings();
+
+	ksft_test_result(ok, "order %d classified\n", order);
+}
+
+int main(void)
+{
+	struct thp_settings settings;
+	unsigned long orders;
+	int order;
+
+	ksft_print_header();
+
+	if (!thp_available())
+		ksft_exit_skip("Transparent Hugepages not available\n");
+
+	pagemap_fd = open("/proc/self/pagemap", O_RDONLY);
+	if (pagemap_fd < 0)
+		ksft_exit_fail_perror("open(/proc/self/pagemap)");
+	kpageflags_fd = open("/proc/kpageflags", O_RDONLY);
+	if (kpageflags_fd < 0)
+		ksft_exit_skip("open(/proc/kpageflags) requires root\n");
+
+	orders = thp_supported_orders();
+	if (!orders)
+		ksft_exit_skip("No supported THP orders\n");
+
+	ksft_set_plan(__builtin_popcountl(orders) + 1);
+
+	thp_save_settings();
+	thp_read_settings(&settings);
+	/* Base of the settings stack; the bottom entry is never popped */
+	thp_push_settings(&settings);
+
+	check_order(0);
+	for (order = 1; order < NR_ORDERS; order++) {
+		if (!(orders & (1UL << order)))
+			continue;
+		check_order(order);
+	}
+
+	ksft_finished();
+}

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 1/5] mm: let folio_mkclean() report which pages had dirty PTEs
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the folio_mkclean() function to report which pages had dirty PTEs by introducing a new function, folio_mkclean_dirtymap(). The latter takes a bitmap and sets a bit for every page of the folio whose entry was dirty. The original folio_mkclean() function is now a wrapper that passes no bitmap, preserving its existing behavior. This change allows downstream code to track which parts of a large folio were written through a mapping, rather than assuming the whole folio changed.

review_comments.author: Usama Arif
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that holding the page-table lock prevents another kernel thread from changing the PTE, but does not prevent the CPU from setting the hardware dirty bit, leading to a timing window where the bitmap is populated from an outdated snapshot of the PTEs. This issue arises in range-aware iomap writeback scenarios and can result in incorrect final dirty state.
review_comments.raw_body:
The patch reads the PTE first and then records pte_dirty(entry) in the bitmap
before invalidating the PTE.

Holding the page-table lock prevents another kernel thread from changing
the PTE, but it does not prevent the CPU from setting the hardware dirty
bit.

This sequence is possible:

  Writeback CPU                  Application CPU
  -------------                  ---------------
  ptep_get(): writable, clean
                                 store through the PTE
                                 hardware sets dirty
  ptep_clear_flush(): returns dirty PTE
  pte_mkclean()
  reinstall clean, read-only PTE

The bitmap was populated from the first, clean snapshot. The dirty state
returned by ptep_clear_flush() is discarded.

With range-aware iomap writeback:

- The folio can still be selected for writeback.
- The affected filesystem block is absent from the iomap dirty bitmap.
- Writeback clears the folio dirty state without writing that block.
- Later eviction can discard the modified data.

The old whole-folio behavior did not need to know which PTE became
dirty, so this timing window was harmless. Sub-folio tracking makes the
final dirty state correctness-critical.

The PMD path has the identical race between pmdp_get() and
pmdp_invalidate().

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 2/5] mm: add a_ops->dirty_folio_range() and use the mkclean dirty harvest
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new operation to the address_space_operations structure called dirty_folio_range(), which allows filesystems to mark specific ranges of a folio as dirty instead of the entire folio. It also introduces a new function folio_mark_dirty_range() that uses this new operation. The patch then updates the folio_clear_dirty_for_io() function to use folio_mkclean_dirtymap() and hand the dirty ranges to the filesystem, reducing unnecessary writes in cases where only part of a folio is modified.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 3/5] mm: keep the mmap dirty range down to the faulting page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch optimizes the way the Linux kernel handles dirty ranges in memory mappings. It reduces the dirty range to a single page when only that page is written, rather than marking the entire folio as dirty. This change improves performance by avoiding unnecessary work and reducing the number of faults that occur due to incorrect dirty state. The patch addresses two specific issues: one where a shared mapping's folio was being marked dirty unnecessarily, and another where a batch of pages was being marked dirty on a write fault, even if only some of those pages were actually written to. The change is made in the `fault_dirty_shared_page` and `set_pte_range` functions, which are responsible for handling faults and page table updates.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 4/5] iomap: narrow page_mkwrite() dirtying to the faulting page
series_items.patch_summary: This patch refactors the iomap code to narrow page_mkwrite() dirtying to only the faulting page, rather than the entire folio. It introduces a new function iomap_dirty_folio_range() that allows for more precise control over which parts of a folio are marked as dirty. The buffered write path and the mmap path now set the dirty range differently, with the latter setting everything due to the whole-folio coverage by iomap_dirty_folio(). The patch also updates several functions to use the new function and corrects some inconsistencies in the code.

series_items.subject: [RFC PATCH 5/5] xfs: track mmap dirty state per block
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the XFS file system to track the dirty state of memory-mapped blocks individually, rather than at the folio (2M) level. This change is made possible by replacing the `dirty_folio` operation with a new `dirty_folio_range` operation that allows for more precise tracking of dirty blocks. As a result, when writing data to a shared mapping, only the affected block is written back instead of the entire folio.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch set introduces sub-folio dirty tracking for PTE-mapped mmap writes, addressing the issue of large page cache folios being dirtied unnecessarily when a single byte is written through a shared file mapping. The problem arises because current implementations mark the entire folio as dirty, leading to inefficient writeback and increased minor fault counts. To solve this, the patch harvests hardware PTE dirty bits at page_mkwrite() time and provides the filesystem with the ranges that were actually modified, allowing for more targeted writeback. This approach is already implemented in XFS and is shown to reduce writeback by 99% on a large file system.

It is always called, but once per folio, not once per page. It is the
filesystem's chance to preallocate whatever it needs to track dirty
state for the *folio*.

Later finish_fault() maps the folio. It tries to map it fully when it
can, so a write fault creates up to 512 writable PTEs on x86. And we
really do need to map the folio fully whenever we can. Otherwise we
significantly undercount mlocked memory. See commit 19773df031bc
("mm/fault: try to map the entire file folio in finish_fault()").

the dirtying to a subset of pages. Any of them can turn dirty at any

review_comments.author: Usama Arif
review_comments.summary: Reviewer noted that holding the page-table lock does not prevent the CPU from setting the hardware dirty bit, creating a timing window where the bitmap is populated from an outdated snapshot of PTEs and the final dirty state correctness-critical.
review_comments.raw_body:
The patch reads the PTE first and then records pte_dirty(entry) in the bitmap
before invalidating the PTE.

Holding the page-table lock prevents another kernel thread from changing
the PTE, but it does not prevent the CPU from setting the hardware dirty
bit.

This sequence is possible:

  Writeback CPU                  Application CPU
  -------------                  ---------------
  ptep_get(): writable, clean
                                 store through the PTE
                                 hardware sets dirty
  ptep_clear_flush(): returns dirty PTE
  pte_mkclean()
  reinstall clean, read-only PTE

The bitmap was populated from the first, clean snapshot. The dirty state
returned by ptep_clear_flush() is discarded.

With range-aware iomap writeback:

- The folio can still be selected for writeback.
- The affected filesystem block is absent from the iomap dirty bitmap.
- Writeback clears the folio dirty state without writing that block.
- Later eviction can discard the modified data.

The old whole-folio behavior did not need to know which PTE became
dirty, so this timing window was harmless. Sub-folio tracking makes the
final dirty state correctness-critical.

The PMD path has the identical race between pmdp_get() and
pmdp_invalidate().

version_history.subject: [PATCH] kernfs: don't hold kernfs_rwsem across notification delivery

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch addresses a performance issue in kernfs where holding the kernfs_rwsem lock across notification delivery causes system daemons to become stuck for long periods of time, especially on multi-tenant systems under memory pressure. The fix involves sampling the name of the kernfs node once before the loop and dropping the lock, allowing other readers to access the kernfs_supers_rwsem list. This change also fixes two potential issues related to file renaming and event naming.

review_comments.author: Tejun Heo
review_comments.summary: Identified the issue and its impact on system performance. Acknowledged the fix as correct and suitable for inclusion in the kernel.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 09, 2026 at 09:54:06PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> Recently at Meta we noticed that on multi-tenant systems, a workload
> under extreme memory pressure negatively impacts unrelated workloads and
> system daemons like below [1] and fb-oomd [2]. Mainly we observed that
> system daemons were stuck on kernfs_rwsem in cgroup-related interfaces
> for long periods of time.
> 
> On further inspection, we found that the workload under pressure had
> registered inotify watches on its memory.events and was continuously
> receiving limit-hitting notifications. The cgroup notification is done in
> kernfs_notify_workfn(), which holds kernfs_supers_rwsem and kernfs_rwsem
> and calls fsnotify(), which allocates the event with
> kmalloc(GFP_KERNEL_ACCOUNT|__GFP_RETRY_MAYFAIL) charged to the watching
> cgroup, which is already under memory pressure. So the notify worker
> ended up in memory reclaim of a cgroup already under pressure, and itself
> kept triggering the limit notifications.
> 
> This notification path takes the locks in read mode, but a waiting writer
> blocks all future readers. That is exactly what is happening in the Meta
> fleet, and it leaves daemons that are critical to the reliability of the
> system stuck for long periods of time.
> 
> Commit 400188ae361a ("kernfs: Acquire kernfs_rwsem in
> kernfs_notify_workfn().") added kernfs_rwsem just to safely read
> kernfs_node::name.  Let's sample the name once before the loop and drop
> the lock.  kernfs_supers_rwsem still covers the list, and the removal
> paths take that one for reading too, so a stalled worker can still hold
> a removal up once a mount or unmount is queued behind it.
> 
> Two things change for a watcher.  A name longer than NAME_MAX now gives
> an event with no name, where before it gave one with the full name;
> fsnotify() takes the name as optional, so the event still arrives.  And
> the name and the parent are no longer sampled under one lock, so a rename
> between the two would name a file against the directory it moved to.
> That cannot happen today: kernfs_notify() rejects anything that is not a
> file, and no caller of kernfs_rename_ns() renames one.
> 
> [1] https://github.com/facebookincubator/below
> [2] https://github.com/facebookincubator/oomd
> 
> Fixes: 400188ae361a ("kernfs: Acquire kernfs_rwsem in kernfs_notify_workfn().")
> Assisted-by: LLM
> Signed-off-by: Shakeel Butt <shakeel.butt@linux.dev>

Acked-by: Tejun Heo <tj@kernel.org>

Thanks.

-- 
tejun

series_items.subject: [PATCH 1/3] kernfs: don't repeat or skip an entry when readdir resumes
series_items.patch_summary: This patch series addresses issues in the kernfs directory implementation, specifically when readdir resumes after an interruption. The current code can repeat or skip entries due to its handling of name hashes and rbtree searches. This patch fixes the issue by restoring a previous behavior where the search for the next entry only continues if the pinned entry is still present.

review_comments.author: Tejun Heo
review_comments.summary: Approved the patch with Acked-by. The reviewer found the explanation clear and the fix reasonable.
review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 09, 2026 at 05:36:48PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> readdir keeps its place as a name hash in ctx->pos and pins the entry in
> file->private_data.  If that entry is gone when the listing comes back,
> kernfs_dir_pos() searches the rbtree for the hash and keeps whatever
> node the descent stopped on.  That is the entry before or after the
> missing one, depending on the shape of the tree.
> 
> Landing before it repeats an entry the previous getdents(2) call already
> reported.  Landing after it, kernfs_dir_next_pos() calls rb_next() and
> steps over an unreported entry.
> 
> With children A(10), B(20), C(30):
> 
>   report A, ctx->pos = 10
>                                     A removed
>   kernfs_dir_next_pos(10, A)
>     A is gone, the search for 10 stops at B
>     rb_next(B) -> C, so B is never reported
> 
> Only the repeat happens today, between two getdents(2) calls.  The skip
> needs the pinned entry to go away inside one call, which the next patch
> allows when it drops kernfs_rwsem around dir_emit().
> 
> Before the commit 4e4d6d860b93 the descent kept a node only on the way
> left, which is a search for the first entry at or after the hash.  That
> commit moved the assignment to the top of the loop, where it runs on
> right turns too.  Restore that search, and step forward only when the
> pinned entry is still there rather than when the hash matches, since two
> entries in one directory can share a hash.
> 
> While here, kernfs_dir_next_pos() called the hash @ino.  It is never an
> inode number, so name it @hash.
> 
> Fixes: 4e4d6d860b93 ("sysfs: Add s_hash to sysfs_dirent and order directory entries by hash")

series_items.subject: [PATCH 3/3] selftests: cover readdir resuming at a removed entry
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds a new test case to the kernfs selftests suite called readdir_resume_at_removed_entry. The test covers the scenario where a directory listing is resumed at an entry that has been removed and then re-added. The test takes a cookie for every entry, removes each one in turn, seeks to its corresponding cookie, and reads the rest of the entries. This ensures that the kernel correctly resumes reading from the correct position after an entry has been removed and re-added.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: The patch series addresses a race condition in kernfs where holding the kernfs_rwsem lock across dir_emit() can lead to readdir skipping or repeating entries, causing issues under memory pressure. The patches propose to copy the name while the lock is held, drop the lock, emit, and take it again, which opens a window for removing the entry that was being listed. Patch 1 closes the race, patch 2 fixes the issue by not holding the lock across dir_emit(), and patch 3 adds tests.

review_comments.raw_body:
On Wed, Sep 09, 2026 at 05:36:48PM -0700, Shakeel Butt wrote:
> readdir keeps its place as a name hash in ctx->pos and pins the entry in
> file->private_data.  If that entry is gone when the listing comes back,
> kernfs_dir_pos() searches the rbtree for the hash and keeps whatever
> node the descent stopped on.  That is the entry before or after the
> missing one, depending on the shape of the tree.
> 
> Landing before it repeats an entry the previous getdents(2) call already
> reported.  Landing after it, kernfs_dir_next_pos() calls rb_next() and
> steps over an unreported entry.
> 
> With children A(10), B(20), C(30):
> 
>   report A, ctx->pos = 10
>                                     A removed
>   kernfs_dir_next_pos(10, A)
>     A is gone, the search for 10 stops at B
>     rb_next(B) -> C, so B is never reported
> 
> Only the repeat happens today, between two getdents(2) calls.  The skip
> needs the pinned entry to go away inside one call, which the next patch
> allows when it drops kernfs_rwsem around dir_emit().
> 
> Before the commit 4e4d6d860b93 the descent kept a node only on the way
> left, which is a search for the first entry at or after the hash.  That
> commit moved the assignment to the top of the loop, where it runs on
> right turns too.  Restore that search, and step forward only when the
> pinned entry is still there rather than when the hash matches, since two
> entries in one directory can share a hash.
> 
> While here, kernfs_dir_next_pos() called the hash @ino.  It is never an
> inode number, so name it @hash.
> 
> Fixes: 4e4d6d860b93 ("sysfs: Add s_hash to sysfs_dirent and order directory entries by hash")

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 1/4] selftests: cover kernfs file handles and same-parent rename
series_items.patch_summary: This patch adds three tests to the kernfs selftest suite: decoding a file handle, decoding while the node is being removed, and looking up a name while an interface is renamed. Additionally, it includes two small fixes: counting only symlinks in ns_tag_isolates_class_net and skipping mkdtemp() failures instead of aborting.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 2/4] kernfs: take kernfs_rename_lock for same-parent renames too
series_items.patch_summary: This patch modifies the kernfs_rename_ns function to take the kernfs_rename_lock lock even when renaming a node within its existing parent directory, not just when moving it to a new parent. This is done to prevent a bug where concurrent renames can create a path that never existed, and also to ensure that readers get a stable name. The patch takes into account the rare occurrence of renames and the fact that the lock is per filesystem, making it a reasonable trade-off for stability.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 3/4] kernfs: don't lose IN_DELETE_SELF when decoding a file handle
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes a bug in the kernfs file system where IN_DELETE_SELF notifications are lost when decoding a file handle. The issue occurs because __kernfs_remove() clears i_nlink on a node's inode, making it invisible to subsequent passes that hash its inode. The patch takes a read lock on kernfs_rwsem to prevent this loss of notification and ensures that the inode is hashed before the ilookup() pass runs. This fix was tested with a 300ms delay between lookup and inode hashing, resulting in st_nlink being correctly set to 0 when removing a file in a cgroup directory.

series_items.subject: [PATCH v2 4/4] kernfs: fix up the unlocked attribute reads on the creation paths
series_items.patch_summary: This patch fixes two issues in the kernfs subsystem related to attribute reads during creation paths. In kernfs_create_link(), the code copies the target's owner attributes without holding a lock, which can lead to inconsistent ownership if the target is modified between the two reads. To fix this, the patch adds a lock to ensure both reads are done under the same lock. In kernfs_new_node(), the code reads the parent's mode and group ID for S_ISGID inheritance without holding a lock, but since the node does not exist yet, taking the lock would only introduce unnecessary contention. Instead, the patch marks these reads with READ_ONCE() to ensure consistency. The changes address issues introduced by a previous commit that allowed creating kernfs objects with arbitrary uid/gid.

patches_submitted.patch_summary: This patch series addresses three independent issues in the kernfs subsystem, including a test coverage update for file handles and same-parent renames. The patches fix bugs related to double put, inode creation, and unlocked attribute reads.
